newsitem.title: USA: US corp bonds track Treasuries, Shopko's off 75 bp.
newsitem.headline: US corp bonds track Treasuries, Shopko's off 75 bp.

text.p: U.S. high-grade corporate bonds slid with U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday, while a spate of fresh paper was said to find strong demand, dealer said.

Punctuating dull secondary trade, traders said at least one issue of ShopKo Stores Inc's outstanding debt widened by 75 basis points after the announced merger of the company and Phar-Mor Inc, traders said.
ShopKo's nine percent senior notes due 2004 were said to trade at a spread of 220 basis points over U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday compared with quoted levels of 145 basis points before the announcement.
Other markets for the paper were not seen, according to several market sources.
Nevertheless, traders said the market was undecided about where the debt would end up with the completion of the merger and possible downgrades by major ratings agencies pending.

"ShopKo bonds are going to widen out dramatically, but there's nothing going on now," one high-grades trader said. "Junk guys are asking where they are, but everybody is evaluating where the credit is going to be and what they're going to do to compensate bondholders if anything. There's a lot of question marks."
Another big shop in New York conceded ShopKo debt would have to come down, but that it did not expect the paper to hit junk bond status.
High-grade secondary trade was otherwise quiet and spreads were mostly unchanged, adding that sellers have not emerged in any significant numbers this week.

Prices were subjected to U.S. Treasury weakness following bearish comments from Federal Reserve governor Janet Yellen, analysts said. Yellen told Reuters the U.S. economy has entered an inflationary danger zone and the Fed must be alert to the risks posed by continued economic expansion.
Yellen also characterized the labor market as "quite tight" labor market conditions. The governor said she sees growth subsiding in the months ahead, but the timing and extent are uncertain.
The 30-year Treasury bond closed down 15/32 at 95-17/32 to yield 7.11 percent.

Back in the corporate arena, new issuance perked up with the emergence of several large deals. Traders said the relatively thin new issue enviroment surrounding the Labor Day holiday ensured demand for the day's deals, which were said to sell briskly.

Goldman Sachs & Co won $150 million 10-year debentures of GTE Hawaiian Telephone via competitive bidding. The debentures were reoffered with a 7.375 percent coupon to yield 7.489 percent, or 57 basis points over the 10-year U.S. Treasury.

Elsewhere, PanEnergy Corp issued $100 million 7.375 percent debentures due 2003 via lead manager J.P. Morgan Securities Inc. The debt was priced to yield 7.383 percent, or 55 basis points over the Treasury curve.

Signet Bank also came to market via J.P. Morgan, pricing $150 million 10-year subordinated bank notes. The notes were given a 7.80 percent coupon and priced to yield 7.836 percent, or 90 basis points over Treasuries.
Key Bank hit the market with a small issue, traders said.

In high-yield secondary trade, Musicland debt continued its downward trend by losing six points on Tuesday on top of a two point loss on Monday, traders said. Musicland's nine percent senior subordinated notes due 2003 were quoted at 28 bid, 34 offered at the close compared with a 34 bid, 40 offered market late Monday.
The broad high-yield market reflected losses of 1/4 point in light dealings, traders said.
